paragraphs: R' Shmuel bar Ami, or Immi.

His father is mentioned in Yevamot ch. 10, halakhah 6: "Immi, the father of Shmuel bar Immi, in the name of R' Yehuda: the halakhah follows R"Sh." And he was the son-in-law of R' Shmuel Saba, as in Sotah 10b, and his father-in-law said [a teaching] in his name. And in Pesachim 16b: "R' Shmuel bar Ami objected to it" — R' Zeira said to him — "R' Shmuel bar Ami accepted it from him, for the Merciful One said," etc.

And in Kiddushin ch. 3, halakhah 2: R"Z said: In the first Adar R' Hila died; in the second Adar a case came before R' Hananiah, the colleague of the rabbis. R' Shmuel bar Ami said to him: Was not R' Hila right in what he told you?

In Yevamot 105a: “Rav Shmuel bar Ami said in the name of R' Yonatan.” Hyman says this should read, “R' Shmuel bar Ami said—and some say Rashbn said—in the name of R' Yonatan,” as in Rosh Hashanah 18a [supplied: כר״ה ית.].
In Avodah Zarah 35a: “Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said, and some say R"Sh (ר״ש) bar Ami.”
Hyman cites Bereshit Rabbah 44:6: R' Abba, R' Berechya and R' Shmuel bar Ami were sitting and raising objections, etc.
He is likewise mentioned in Midrash Shmuel 5:2.
And in Niddah 20b: "Ami bar Shmuel" — but Hyman says he is not his son, since this Ami was a student of Shmuel.

notes.text: כר״ה יח. is a citation to Rosh Hashanah18a, not an unnamed person followed by ית. The named Avodah Zarah35a text reads Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi and, alternatively, Rabbi Shimon bar Ami; Hyman’s notice supplies Shmuel bar Ami, so this remains an explicit attribution difference.

Only the first expansion is used in the body; the second remains R"Sh (ר״ש) bar Ami because the supplied notice abbreviates both names and its placement under Shmuel does not establish which name Hyman intended. The heading explicitly spells רבי, so its full Rabbi remains; p001 abbreviates ר׳ and retains R'. Full Rav in the reported Yevamot105a reading remains, while unsupported Yehuda, Shmuel Saba, Zeira, Hila, Hananiah, Yonatan, Abba, Berechya and contextual Shmuel occurrences keep R'. Full titles in the Avodah Zarah scalar are not transferred to other passages. R"Sh in the first Yevamot law, R"Z in Kiddushin and Rashbn in the alternative chain remain visibly abbreviated. The printed notice (volume III, pp. 1135–1136) gives Pesachim 16b, beside the supplied Hebrew’s 15b. The English locator follows the print and the directly consulted 16b exchange: Rav Shmuel bar Ami objects, Rabbi Zeira replies, and Shmuel accepts the reply. The source’s abbreviated titles remain; full titles in the direct witness are not transferred globally. The print also gives Rosh Hashanah 18a, beside supplied כר״ה ית. The consulted Rosh passage has Rav Shmuel bar Ami and an alternative Rav Shmuel bar Nachmani reporting Rav Yonatan; Yevamot 105a has Rav Shmuel bar Ami reporting Rabbi Yonatan. Hyman’s definite proposal to change Rav to the abbreviated Rabbi form remains his emendation. Sotah 10b directly describes Shmuel Saba as Shmuel bar Ami’s father-in-law and has him report in his son-in-law’s name. Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 10:6 names Immi as Shmuel’s father and gives Rav Yehudah in the chain. The full Kiddushin 3:2 case preserves the two Adars; Guggenheimer translates לא יאות as the negative statement that Hila was wrong, whereas the retained English follows the rhetorical-question interpretation. That interpretive difference remains open. Avodah Zarah 35a spells out Shimon bar Ami, so the ambiguous R-Sh in Hyman’s clause remains visible. Midrash Shmuel 5:2 directly names Shmuel bar Immi; Niddah 20b names Rav Ami bar Shmuel without establishing Hyman’s rejection of a father-son identification or his student chronology. The supplied Bereshit Rabbah 44:6 report remains Hyman’s citation: the consulted section is a different discussion, and a bounded nonmatch does not prove absence from another edition. No name or identity has been harmonized, and the existing notes remain verbatim.
